rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 and Tables 4-7 report the authors' own greenhouse experiment (tomato and cucumber, Beijing, spring and autumn 2016) with micro-nano bubble water oxygation delivered through subsurface drip irrigation.
rows.notes: The study does not show that aerated drip irrigation conserves soil moisture or saves water and fertilizer. Section 2.2 states irrigation quota and fertilizer were identical in all treatments, and Section 3.2 says soil water content and evaporation were assumed approximately equal and not measured; the only water-related result is higher IWUE (Table 5), which the authors attribute entirely to higher yield at equal water input. Soil moisture was not measured and no water or fertilizer saving was tested.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 describe the authors' own greenhouse field experiment with MNB water oxygation via SDI. Q2: Table 5 and Section 3.2 report irrigation water use efficiency of tomato and cucumber under oxygation treatments versus the non-oxygated control, with IWUE increases of up to 16.9% (tomato) and 22.1% (cucumber) in the optimal treatments (Abstract, Conclusions). Q4: Section 2.3.3 and Fig. 3 report measured soil oxygen content in the root zone for three treatments, and Section 4.1 reports that MNBWO raised and stabilised soil oxygen within 24 h; Table 4 reports root dry weight, the intermediate pathway by which oxygation raises yield and hence IWUE. Q9: Table 5 reports IWUE means with <U+00B1> dispersion values for every treatment and season.
rows.notes: Evidence for 'water conservation' is limited to higher IWUE at equal irrigation volume; no water was actually saved and soil water was not measured (Section 3.2). Q3: single method (plot measurements), no. Q5: one soil, one greenhouse, two crops, two seasons, no. Q6: greenhouse plots only. Q7: authors recommend mixing ratio and 5-day frequency and say 7-day is 'overly long', but these are optimisation/recommendation statements rather than stated requirements for the effect; conservatively no. Q8: only 'needs further investigation' statements on fruit quality mechanism and a missing cucumber vitamin C dataset; no stated limitation on the IWUE result.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 describe the authors' own greenhouse experiment (3x3 factorial, four replicates) with MNB oxygation via SDI. Q2: Table 5 and Section 3.2 report that tomato and cucumber yields increased significantly under MNBWO relative to the control, e.g. tomato M1/4 at F1/5 was 16.9% above control and cucumber M1/0 at F1/5 was 22.1% above control; Section 4.1 summarises yield increases of 7.8-26.9% (tomato) and 2.3-16.3% (cucumber). Q4: Section 2.3.3 and Fig. 3 report measured root-zone soil oxygen content under different mixing ratios, and Table 4 reports root and shoot dry matter, the mechanism through which oxygation increases yield (Section 4.1). Q9: Table 5 reports yield means with <U+00B1> dispersion for every treatment and season.
rows.notes: Q3: one method only. Q5: single site, single loam soil, two crops, two seasons. Q6: plot scale in one greenhouse. Q7: recommended mixing ratios differ by crop and frequency of 5 d is said to be best, but these are reported as optima/recommendations rather than stated preconditions for the yield effect; interaction and crop-sensitivity differences are speculated ('it was speculated'). Q8: no limitation stated on the yield result; only 'must be investigated further' for quality mechanism.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 describe the authors' own greenhouse experiment on MNB water oxygation via SDI. Q2: Table 5 and Section 3.2 report both yield and IWUE of tomato and cucumber under oxygation versus control, with significant increases (optimal treatment: +16.9% yield and IWUE for tomato, +22.1% for cucumber; Abstract and Conclusions). Q4: Section 2.3.3 and Fig. 3 report measured soil oxygen content in the root zone, and Table 4 root/shoot dry matter, the intermediate variables through which aeration raises yield and WUE (Section 4.1). Q9: Table 5 gives yield and WUE means with <U+00B1> dispersion for all treatments.
rows.notes: IWUE gain is entirely yield-driven because irrigation volume was equal across treatments (Section 3.2). Q3: single method. Q5: one soil/site, two crops. Q6: greenhouse plots. Q7: optimal mixing ratio and frequency are given as recommendations, not stated as requirements. Q8: no limitation stated on the yield/WUE result.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study is a single-site greenhouse experiment (loam soil, Beijing) on micro-nano bubble oxygation through subsurface drip irrigation for tomato and cucumber across two seasons in 2016; irrigation and fertilizer inputs were identical across treatments so IWUE differences reflect yield only. Soil oxygen was measured only for the three F1/5 treatments.
